claim: Cells are organized by functional modules, which typically contain components whose removal severely compromises the module's function.
source: Cells are organized by functional modules, which typically contain components whose removal severely compromises the module's function.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell organization presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Important components of functional modules are not absolutely conserved between parts of the tree of life.
source: Despite their importance, these components are not absolutely conserved between parts of the tree of life, suggesting that cells can evolve to perform the same biological functions with different proteins.
evidence: This statement is presented as an observation from comparative biology, suggesting it draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Cells can evolve to perform the same biological functions with different proteins.
source: Despite their importance, these components are not absolutely conserved between parts of the tree of life, suggesting that cells can evolve to perform the same biological functions with different proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation about lack of conservation across the tree of life.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae was evolved for 1000 generations without the polarity gene BEM1.
source: We evolved Saccharomyces cerevisiae for 1000 generations without the important polarity gene BEM1.
evidence: This describes the experimental design performed by the authors.

claim: bem1∆ lineages rapidly increase in fitness initially.
source: Initially the bem1∆ lineages rapidly increase in fitness and then slowly reach >90% of the fitness of their BEM1 ancestors at the end of the evolution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of growth rates over time.

claim: bem1∆ lineages reach >90% of the fitness of their BEM1 ancestors at the end of the evolution.
source: Initially the bem1∆ lineages rapidly increase in fitness and then slowly reach >90% of the fitness of their BEM1 ancestors at the end of the evolution.
evidence: This is supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The bem1∆ lineages follow a common evolutionary trajectory with a fixed sequence of adaptive mutations.
source: Sequencing their genomes and monitoring polarization reveals a common evolutionary trajectory, with a fixed sequence of adaptive mutations, each improving cell polarization by inactivating proteins.
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data and Sanger sequencing showing the order of mutations.

claim: Each adaptive mutation in the bem1∆ lineages improves cell polarization by inactivating proteins.
source: Sequencing their genomes and monitoring polarization reveals a common evolutionary trajectory, with a fixed sequence of adaptive mutations, each improving cell polarization by inactivating proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of nonsense mutations and the phenotypic analysis of reconstructed strains.

claim: Organisms can be evolutionarily robust to physiologically destructive perturbations.
source: Our results show that organisms can be evolutionarily robust to physiologically destructive perturbations and suggest that recovery by gene inactivation can lead to rapid divergence in the parts list for cell biologically important functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that bem1∆ cells recovered fitness through evolution.

claim: Recovery by gene inactivation can lead to rapid divergence in the parts list for cell biologically important functions.
source: Our results show that organisms can be evolutionarily robust to physiologically destructive perturbations and suggest that recovery by gene inactivation can lead to rapid divergence in the parts list for cell biologically important functions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: A biochemical and biophysical picture is emerging of how cell polarization and movement modules self-organize.
source: In cell polarization and movement, a biochemical and biophysical picture is emerging of how those complex functional modules self-organize to accomplish their functions (Howard et al., 2011; Goehring and Grill, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Components essential for a module in well-studied model organisms can be absent in evolutionarily distant organisms.
source: Surprisingly, components that are essential for a module in well-studied model organisms can be absent in evolutionarily distant organisms (Bergmiller et al., 2012), even though the modules must perform the same tasks.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous comparative work.

claim: Complex modules reorganize during evolution to accommodate changing requirements or respond to chance loss of components during population bottlenecks.
source: This observation suggests that complex modules reorganize during evolution, either to accommodate changing requirements or to respond to the chance loss of components during population bottlenecks, when selection against deleterious mutations is greatly diminished.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about component absence in distant organisms.

claim: Experimental microbial evolution allows identification of mutations responsible for selected phenotypes and their temporal order.
source: Experimental microbial evolution circumvents these problems: sequencing and genetic analysis identifies the mutations responsible for the selected phenotype and storing and analyzing intermediate steps reveals the order in which mutations occurred (Lenski and Travisano, 1994; Lang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental evolution studies.

claim: Selections for faster growth or novel functions typically produce adaptive mutations in multiple functional modules.
source: In principle, these tools should lead to mechanistic understanding of evolutionary trajectories, but selections for faster growth or novel functions typically produce adaptive mutations in multiple functional modules (Kvitek and Sherlock, 2013), whose relationship to each other is hard to explain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Yeast cells polarize and bud by localizing and activating the small GTPase Cdc42 at a single site.
source: Yeast cells polarize and bud by localizing and activating the small GTPase, Cdc42, at a single site (Slaughter et al., 2009b; Wu and Lew, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on yeast polarization.

claim: In haploid cells, polarization is directed by a historical mark deposited in the previous cell cycle.
source: In haploid cells, polarization is directed by a historical mark deposited in the previous cell cycle, but even when the mark is absent, yeast cells still polarize efficiently, albeit at a random location (Chant and Herskowitz, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When the historical mark is absent, yeast cells still polarize efficiently at a random location.
source: In haploid cells, polarization is directed by a historical mark deposited in the previous cell cycle, but even when the mark is absent, yeast cells still polarize efficiently, albeit at a random location (Chant and Herskowitz, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Symmetry breaking in yeast polarization depends on an actin-based mechanism involving positive feedback between actin-mediated delivery of Cdc42 and actin polymerization stimulated by membrane-bound Cdc42.
source: Under these conditions, symmetry breaking depends on at least two pathways: (1) an actin-based mechanism based on the positive feedback between actin-mediated delivery of Cdc42 to the plasma membrane and actin polymerization stimulated by membrane-bound Cdc42 (Wedlich-Soldner et al., 2003; Marco et al., 2007; Freisinger et al., 2013; Slaughter et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Symmetry breaking in yeast polarization depends on an actin independent, Turing type mechanism involving interactions amongst proteins that regulate Cdc42 activity and localization.
source: and (2) an actin independent, Turing type mechanism that depends on interactions amongst proteins that regulate the activity and localization of Cdc42 (Howell et al., 2012; Freisinger et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: Bem1 is a regulator of Cdc42 that recruits the guanine exchange factor Cdc24 and Cdc42 to the membrane.
source: We strongly perturbed yeast polarization by removing Bem1, a regulator of Cdc42, which recruits the guanine exchange factor (GEF) Cdc24 as well as Cdc42 to the membrane where Cdc24 activates membrane-bound Cdc42.
evidence: This describes the known function of Bem1 based on established knowledge.

claim: Bem1 is a relatively young component in polarity establishment that had a different role in ancestral fungi.
source: We decided to delete Bem1 because previous research suggests that this protein is a relatively young component in polarity establishment that had a different role in ancestral fungi (Semighini and Harris, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: bem1∆ spores formed colonies at a frequency of 6 ± 0.4 × 10−5.
source: bem1∆ spores formed colonies at a frequency of 6 ± 0.4 × 10−5 (Figure 1B, for details see Supplementary materials)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Wild-type (BEM1) spores formed colonies at a frequency of 0.95.
source: while wild-type (BEM1) spores formed colonies at a frequency of 0.95.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment.

claim: The majority of bem1∆ cells (28/35) did not polarize within 500 min.
source: The majority of bem1∆ cells (28/35 vs 0/41 for wild-type cells) did not polarize within 500 min but grew isotropically resulting in very large cells (Figure 1C) that often lysed (16/35) (Video 2).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and counting from microscopy experiments.

claim: bem1∆ cells that did not polarize within 500 min grew isotropically resulting in very large cells.
source: The majority of bem1∆ cells (28/35 vs 0/41 for wild-type cells) did not polarize within 500 min but grew isotropically resulting in very large cells (Figure 1C) that often lysed (16/35) (Video 2).
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations shown in Figure 1C and Video 2.

claim: 16 out of 35 bem1∆ cells lysed.
source: The majority of bem1∆ cells (28/35 vs 0/41 for wild-type cells) did not polarize within 500 min but grew isotropically resulting in very large cells (Figure 1C) that often lysed (16/35) (Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct count from microscopy observations.

claim: The probability of bem1∆ cells polarizing is 0.23.
source: The bem1∆ cells that did polarize, (Figure 1D, Ppolarize_bem1∆ = 0.23, N = 35), polarize fast
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: bem1∆ cells that do polarize, polarize fast.
source: The bem1∆ cells that did polarize, (Figure 1D, Ppolarize_bem1∆ = 0.23, N = 35), polarize fast, in contrast to wild-type cells, which show a wider distribution of polarization times, but always eventually polarize successfully (Figure 1D, Ppolarize_wt = 1, N = 41).
evidence: This is observed from the distribution shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Wild-type cells show a wider distribution of polarization times but always eventually polarize successfully.
source: The bem1∆ cells that did polarize, (Figure 1D, Ppolarize_bem1∆ = 0.23, N = 35), polarize fast, in contrast to wild-type cells, which show a wider distribution of polarization times, but always eventually polarize successfully (Figure 1D, Ppolarize_wt = 1, N = 41).
evidence: This is observed from the distribution shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The probability of wild-type cells polarizing is 1.
source: The bem1∆ cells that did polarize, (Figure 1D, Ppolarize_bem1∆ = 0.23, N = 35), polarize fast, in contrast to wild-type cells, which show a wider distribution of polarization times, but always eventually polarize successfully (Figure 1D, Ppolarize_wt = 1, N = 41).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ten bem1∆ cultures and ten wild-type cultures were evolved for one thousand generations by serial dilutions.
source: From both colonies, we started with 10 wild-type and 10 bem1∆ cultures, which we evolved for one thousand generations by serial dilutions, regularly freezing down a sample (Figure 2A and see Materials and methods)
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nine bem1∆ lineages and seven wild-type lineages survived the evolution experiment.
source: resulting (due to contamination) in nine surviving bem1∆ lineages and seven wild-type lineages.
evidence: This is a direct count of the surviving lineages.

claim: The initial growth rate of the bem1∆ lineages was approximately 12 times lower than the wild-type growth rate.
source: The initial growth rate of the bem1∆ lineages was approximately 12 times lower than the wild-type growth rate.
evidence: This is calculated from growth rate measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: By the end of the experiment, the bem1∆ cells grew at almost the rate of their wild-type ancestors.
source: By the end of the experiment, however, the bem1∆ cells grew at almost the rate of their wild-type ancestors (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by the growth rate measurements in Figure 2B.

claim: Cells that take longer to polarize are on average larger than cells that polarize fast because yeast cells continue to grow during polarity establishment.
source: We examined how the cell size distribution, which is an approximation for polarization dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), changed during the experiment: cells that take longer to polarize are on average larger than cells that polarize fast because yeast cells continue to grow during polarity establishment (Goranov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and the relationship shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: At the beginning of the experiment, bem1∆ cells were larger and showed a wider distribution than the wild-type ancestor.
source: At the beginning of the experiment, bem1∆ cells were larger and showed a wider distribution than the wild-type ancestor (Figure 2C,E,F) as confirmed by microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1 and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown by cell size measurements and microscopy images in multiple figures.

claim: At the end of the experiment, both the mode and the standard deviation in bem1∆ cells adapted to wild-type cell size.
source: At the end of the experiment, however, both the mode and the standard deviation in bem1∆ cells adapted to wild-type cell size (Figure 2D) and growth rate values, suggesting a properly functioning polarization machinery.
evidence: This is shown by cell size measurements in Figure 2D.

claim: The adaptation of bem1∆ cells to wild-type cell size and growth rate suggests a properly functioning polarization machinery.
source: At the end of the experiment, however, both the mode and the standard deviation in bem1∆ cells adapted to wild-type cell size (Figure 2D) and growth rate values, suggesting a properly functioning polarization machinery.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cell size and growth rate data.

claim: Five wild-type lines were sequenced from the seven that survived at the end of the evolution experiment.
source: We sequenced the whole genomes of several evolved lines: from the seven wild-type lines that were left at the end of the evolution experiment, we sequenced five lines.
evidence: This describes the sequencing approach taken.

claim: A total of 10 bem1∆ lines were sequenced.
source: We sequenced a total of 10 bem1∆ lines: the eight bem1∆ A-lines that arose from the same starting colony and remained haploid, as described above. In addition, we sequenced two bem1∆ lines that were evolved from two independent different starting colonies in a trial experiment (T2 and T3) (Laan et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the sequencing approach taken.

claim: In the control wild-type lines, a diverse set of mutations was found with only one gene, ECM21, being mutated twice.
source: In the control, wild-type lines we found a diverse set of mutations (Supplementary file 1), with only one gene, ECM21, being mutated twice.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: ECM21 was the only mutated gene in the control lines that was also found in either of two other large scale evolution experiments.
source: ECM21 was also the only mutated gene, in our control lines, that was also found in either of two other large scale evolution experiments (Lang et al., 2013; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014)
evidence: This is based on comparison with published sequencing data from other studies.

claim: Adaptation in the control experiments involves similar mutations to those in other studies that have led to modest increases in the proliferation rate of wild-type cells.
source: suggesting that adaptation in our control experiments involves similar mutations to those in other studies that have led to modest increases in the proliferation rate of wild-type cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with other evolution experiments.

claim: BEM3 was mutated in 10 out of 10 bem1∆ lines.
source: We found three genes that were mutated at least three times: BEM3 (10/10), NRP1 (5/10), and BEM2 (3/10).
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: NRP1 was mutated in 5 out of 10 bem1∆ lines.
source: We found three genes that were mutated at least three times: BEM3 (10/10), NRP1 (5/10), and BEM2 (3/10).
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: BEM2 was mutated in 3 out of 10 bem1∆ lines.
source: We found three genes that were mutated at least three times: BEM3 (10/10), NRP1 (5/10), and BEM2 (3/10).
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Mutations in BEM3, NRP1, and BEM2 were not reported in a variety of other yeast evolution experiments.
source: Mutations in these genes were not reported in a variety of other yeast evolution experiments (Gresham et al., 2008; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011; Koschwanez et al., 2013; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2013; Lang et al., 2013; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014), suggesting that they are specific for the deletion of BEM1.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data from other evolution experiments.

claim: Mutations in BEM3, NRP1, and BEM2 are specific for the deletion of BEM1.
source: Mutations in these genes were not reported in a variety of other yeast evolution experiments (Gresham et al., 2008; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011; Koschwanez et al., 2013; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2013; Lang et al., 2013; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014), suggesting that they are specific for the deletion of BEM1.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of these mutations in other evolution experiments.

claim: The mutation in IRA1 in line T3 is commonly found in other yeast evolution experiments.
source: Only one of these mutations, the mutation in IRA1, in line T3, is also commonly found in other yeast evolution experiments suggesting that it is not specific for the deletion of BEM1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data from other evolution experiments.

claim: The A-lines shared the same early stop mutation in BEM3.
source: The A-lines shared the same early stop mutation in BEM3, but lines T2 and T3 independently acquired different early stop mutations in BEM3.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Lines T2 and T3 independently acquired different early stop mutations in BEM3.
source: The A-lines shared the same early stop mutation in BEM3, but lines T2 and T3 independently acquired different early stop mutations in BEM3.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The BEM3 mutation in the A-lines (Q61*) was acquired after germination of the spore that acted as their ancestor.
source: The BEM3 mutation in the A-lines (Q61*) was acquired after germination of the spore that acted as their ancestor: cells from the original colony (Video 3) showed the same severe growth defects as freshly germinated bem1∆ spores, whereas engineered bem1∆ bem3∆ cells had a much less severe defect.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the phenotype of the original colony with engineered double mutants.

claim: All five mutations in NRP1 were independently acquired early stop mutations.
source: All five mutations in NRP1 (all in A-lines) were independently acquired early stop mutations
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: In BEM2, a promoter mutation was found in line T2 and two amino acid substitutions were found in lines A1 and A2.
source: whereas in BEM2 we found a promoter mutation (line T2) and two amino acid substitutions (line A1 and A2), which are radical substitutions at conserved positions.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The amino acid substitutions in BEM2 are radical substitutions at conserved positions.
source: whereas in BEM2 we found a promoter mutation (line T2) and two amino acid substitutions (line A1 and A2), which are radical substitutions at conserved positions.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the mutations.

claim: In lines A1 and A2, mutations occurred sequentially in BEM3, NRP1, and BEM2.
source: Lines A1 and A2 acquired mutations in BEM2, BEM3, and NRP1. Sanger sequencing of the three genes at different time points revealed that those mutations occurred sequentially in BEM3, NRP1, and BEM2 in both lines (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on Sanger sequencing at different time points shown in Figure 3B.

claim: bem1∆ spores are least likely to form colonies among the tested genotypes.
source: Figure 3C shows that bem1∆ spores are least likely to form colonies
evidence: This is shown by the colony formation data in Figure 3C.

claim: bem1∆ bem2∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆ spores closely resemble wild-type spores in colony formation.
source: while bem1∆ bem2∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆ spores closely resemble wild-type spores, confirming that inactivating BEM2, BEM3, and NRP1 substantially suppresses the severe polarization defect of bem1∆ cells.
evidence: This is shown by the colony formation data in Figure 3C.

claim: Inactivating BEM2, BEM3, and NRP1 substantially suppresses the severe polarization defect of bem1∆ cells.
source: while bem1∆ bem2∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆ spores closely resemble wild-type spores, confirming that inactivating BEM2, BEM3, and NRP1 substantially suppresses the severe polarization defect of bem1∆ cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the colony formation and growth rate data.

claim: The growth rate of line A2 is indistinguishable from the reconstructed strain carrying gene deletions in the genes that were mutated.
source: The growth rate of line A2 is indistinguishable from the reconstructed strain, which carries gene deletions in the genes that were mutated in our experiments, suggesting that we found the mutations that confer fitness to this lineage
evidence: This is based on growth rate measurements comparing evolved and reconstructed strains.

claim: Line A1 grows slightly faster than the quadruple mutant, suggesting it may contain additional adaptive mutations.
source: but line A1 grows slightly faster than the quadruple mutant, suggesting that it may contain additional adaptive mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth rate comparison.

claim: Adding the bem2∆ mutation increases the growth rate of bem1∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆ cells.
source: adding the bem2∆ mutation increases the growth rate of bem1∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆ cells, but the same mutation reduces or has no effect on the fitness of all other tested genotypes.
evidence: This is shown by the growth rate measurements in Figure 3C.

claim: The bem2∆ mutation reduces or has no effect on the fitness of all other tested genotypes besides bem1∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆.
source: adding the bem2∆ mutation increases the growth rate of bem1∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆ cells, but the same mutation reduces or has no effect on the fitness of all other tested genotypes.
evidence: This is shown by the growth rate measurements in Figure 3C.

claim: The polarization module evolves from requiring Bem1 in wild-type strains to being slightly impaired by the presence of functional Bem1 in a bem2∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆ mutant.
source: Another example of epistasis is the changing dependence of the cells on BEM1: the polarization module evolves from requiring Bem1, in wild-type strains, to being slightly impaired by the presence of functional Bem1 in a bem2∆ bem3∆ nrp1∆ mutant (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing growth rates of strains with and without BEM1 in different genetic backgrounds in Figure 3D.

claim: bem1∆ cells have a long delay before the first signs of polarization.
source: As expected, bem1∆ cells have a long delay before the first signs of polarization, and polarization is often abortive (Video 5, Figure 4C), suggesting weaker activation of Cdc42.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Video 5 and Figure 4C.

claim: Polarization in bem1∆ cells is often abortive.
source: As expected, bem1∆ cells have a long delay before the first signs of polarization, and polarization is often abortive (Video 5, Figure 4C), suggesting weaker activation of Cdc42.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Video 5 and Figure 4C.

claim: The long delay and abortive polarization in bem1∆ cells suggests weaker activation of Cdc42.
source: As expected, bem1∆ cells have a long delay before the first signs of polarization, and polarization is often abortive (Video 5, Figure 4C), suggesting weaker activation of Cdc42.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the polarization dynamics.

claim: bem1∆ cells often contain more than one polarity site.
source: In addition, bem1∆ cells often contain more than one polarity site, suggesting that the positive feedback that ensures a single site of polarization is weaker.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Video 5 and Figure 4C.

claim: The presence of multiple polarity sites in bem1∆ cells suggests that the positive feedback that ensures a single site of polarization is weaker.
source: In addition, bem1∆ cells often contain more than one polarity site, suggesting that the positive feedback that ensures a single site of polarization is weaker.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of multiple polarity sites.

claim: BEM3 and BEM2 encode two of the four GAPs in the polarity module that inactivate Cdc42 and other small G proteins.
source: BEM3 and BEM2 encode two of the four GAPs (GTPase Activating Proteins) in the polarity module that inactivate Cdc42 (Zheng et al., 1994) and other small G proteins by stimulating their intrinsic GTPase activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Inactivating BEM3 and BEM2 should increase Cdc42 activity.
source: Inactivating these genes should increase Cdc42 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of BEM3 and BEM2 as GAPs.

claim: bem1∆ bem3∆ cells bud faster than bem1∆ cells.
source: As predicted, bem1∆ bem3∆ cells bud faster (Video 6, Figure 4C)
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Video 6 and Figure 4C.

claim: bem1∆ bem3∆ cells still often contain more than one polarity site.
source: but the cells still often contain more than one polarity site, suggesting that increasing Cdc42 activity is not enough to re-establish precise positive feedback in the absence of Bem1.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Video 6 and Figure 4C.

claim: Increasing Cdc42 activity is not enough to re-establish precise positive feedback in the absence of Bem1.
source: but the cells still often contain more than one polarity site, suggesting that increasing Cdc42 activity is not enough to re-establish precise positive feedback in the absence of Bem1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bem1∆ bem3∆ cells still have multiple polarity sites.

claim: NRP1 is an RNA binding protein that localizes to stress granules.
source: Less is known about NRP1, an RNA binding protein that localizes to stress granules and has not been related to polarity before (Buchan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: NRP1 has not been related to polarity before this study.
source: Less is known about NRP1, an RNA binding protein that localizes to stress granules and has not been related to polarity before (Buchan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on the literature.

claim: A high-throughput RNA binding study suggested seven target RNAs for NRP1.
source: A high-throughput RNA binding study suggested seven target RNAs for NRP1, but none of them forms an obvious link to polarity, and most have an unknown function (Hogan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: None of the seven target RNAs for NRP1 forms an obvious link to polarity.
source: A high-throughput RNA binding study suggested seven target RNAs for NRP1, but none of them forms an obvious link to polarity, and most have an unknown function (Hogan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cited study.

claim: The most obvious change after NRP1 deletion is a decrease in time between cytokinesis and the appearance of the first polarity site.
source: The most obvious change after NRP1 deletion is a decrease in time between cytokinesis and the appearance of the first polarity site (Video 7, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Video 7 and Figure 4C.

claim: NRP1 may play a role in initiating polarization triggered by Cdc28 activation.
source: Therefore, we speculate that NRP1 plays a role in initiating polarization, which is triggered when Cdc28 is activated by G1 cyclins.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed phenotype.

claim: The loss of Bem2 reduces the time that cells are not polarized.
source: Finally, the loss of Bem2 reduces the time that the cells are not polarized, suggesting that this mutation also increases Cdc42 activity (Video 8).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy data in Video 8 and Figure 4C.

claim: The loss of Bem2 suggests that this mutation increases Cdc42 activity.
source: Finally, the loss of Bem2 reduces the time that the cells are not polarized, suggesting that this mutation also increases Cdc42 activity (Video 8).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed phenotype and the known function of Bem2 as a GAP.

claim: Multiple mutations can restore Cdc42 activity without restoring Bem1's ability to physically connect Cdc24 and Cdc42.
source: Our data suggest that that multiple mutations can restore Cdc42 activity without restoring Bem1's ability to physically connect Cdc24 and Cdc42.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells recover without BEM1 through mutations in other genes.

claim: Actin-based positive feedback will become critical in the absence of Bem1 because actin-independent polarization depends directly on Bem1 acting as a scaffold.
source: As a consequence, actin-based positive feedback, which only requires Bem1 to activate Cdc42, will become critical because actin-independent polarization depends directly on Bem1 acting as a scaffold.
evidence: This is inferred from the known mechanisms of polarization.

claim: When actin-based positive feedback acts alone, it creates multiple simultaneous polarity sites.
source: Previous work showed that when actin-based positive feedback acts alone, it creates multiple simultaneous polarity sites (Freisinger et al., 2013), as we observe in our mutants.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and confirmed by observations in this study.

claim: Cells recovered by following a reproducible evolutionary trajectory that could be largely explained by the interactions amongst the mutated genes.
source: Cells recovered by following a reproducible evolutionary trajectory that could be largely explained by the interactions amongst the mutated genes and led to a substantial recovery in the speed and accuracy of cell polarization.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The evolutionary trajectory led to a substantial recovery in the speed and accuracy of cell polarization.
source: Cells recovered by following a reproducible evolutionary trajectory that could be largely explained by the interactions amongst the mutated genes and led to a substantial recovery in the speed and accuracy of cell polarization.
evidence: This is shown by the growth rate and polarization dynamics measurements.

claim: Experimental evolution has produced a range of answers to the question of how repeatable evolution is.
source: How repeatable is evolution? Experimental evolution has produced a range of answers to this question, from replicate populations that share a small fraction of causal mutations (Gresham et al., 2008; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011; Chou and Marx, 2012; Koschwanez et al., 2013; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014) to those where mutations occur in the same genes in the same order (Blount et al., 2012; Herron and Doebeli, 2013) or repeatedly affect the same amino acids in a protein (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: For multiple substitutions in the same protein, strong epistasis can render most trajectories impossible or unlikely.
source: For multiple substitutions, in the same protein, strong epistasis can render most trajectories impossible or unlikely (Weinreich et al., 2006; Bridgham et al., 2009; Hinkley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Pseudomonas fluorescens, loss-of-function mutations are most frequent and other pathways can only be found when the dominant pathway is blocked.
source: Examining the mutations that gave rise to a particular phenotype in the bacterium, Pseudomonas fluorescens, revealed a hierarchy of pathways: loss-of-function mutations are most frequent and other pathways, including promoter mutations, gene fusions, and gain-of-function mutations can only be found when the dominant pathway is blocked (Lind et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: This is the first example of reproducible trajectories to adaptation to mutations that severely compromise a cellular function.
source: As far as we know, this is the first example of reproducible trajectories to adaptation to mutations that severely compromise a cellular function, and it will be interesting to see if evolving strains, adapting to severe perturbations in other pathways will also lead to reproducible trajectories.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The multiple layers of regulation that allow cells to polarize rapidly and accurately also make it possible for them to adapt by evolution to very strong perturbations.
source: We interpret our results as demonstrating that the multiple layers of regulation that allow cells to polarize rapidly and accurately also make it possible for them to adapt, by evolution, to very strong perturbations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Under strong selective pressure, the larger target size for mutations that inactivate proteins favors evolutionary trajectories that remove components from modules over those that quantitatively alter their properties.
source: Under strong selective pressure, the larger target size for mutations that inactivate proteins favors evolutionary trajectories that remove components from modules over those that quantitatively alter their properties.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why loss-of-function mutations were selected.

claim: Removing regulators like Bem2 and Bem3 is the equivalent of rarer mutations that would change the biochemical parameters of central components of the pathway.
source: As long as modules contain components, like Bem2 and Bem3, which alter the quantitative behavior of other proteins, like Cdc42 and other small GTPases, removing the regulators is the equivalent of rarer mutations that would change the biochemical parameters of central components of the pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional consequences of the mutations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations allow bacteria and yeast to adapt to their environments.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous experimental evolution work which showed that loss-of-function mutations allow bacteria (Zinser et al., 2003; Hottes et al., 2013) and yeast (Koschwanez et al., 2013) to adapt to their environments and produce novel phenotypes (Wildenberg and Murray, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Adaptation by loss-of-function mutations has been observed in natural populations.
source: Adaptation by loss-of-function mutations has also been observed in natural populations (Maurelli et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2006; Bliven and Maurelli, 2012; D'Souza et al., 2014, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The selected mutations do not alter the structure of an existing protein to allow it to play Bem1's role of physically linking Cdc42 to Cdc24.
source: In our work, the selected mutations do not alter the structure of an existing protein to allow it to play Bem1's role of physically linking Cdc42 to Cdc24.
evidence: This is based on the nature of the mutations identified (nonsense mutations and deletions).

claim: Mutations that increase the half-life of Cdc42-GTP remove the need to hold Cdc24 and Cdc42 close to each other.
source: Instead, other mutations that increase the half-life of Cdc42-GTP (and possibly other small G proteins) remove the need to hold Cdc24 and Cdc42 close to each other.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the mutations compensate for the loss of Bem1.

claim: If increasing the dosage of genes can reverse the effects of a perturbation, cells may recover by becoming aneuploid.
source: If increasing the dosage of genes can reverse the effects of the perturbation, cells may recover by becoming aneuploid, as observed when duplicating chromosome XVI increases the dosage of two genes (MKK2 and RLM1) that help compensate for the absence of type II myosin (Rancati et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: If removing inhibitors will increase fitness, point mutations that inactivate the inhibitors will be selected.
source: In contrast, if removing inhibitors will increase fitness, point mutations that inactivate the inhibitors will be selected, as we observed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Certain eukaryotic lineages lack extremely well-conserved pathways, such as the absence of the anaphase promoting complex from Giardia.
source: Our results may help to explain the surprising observation that certain eukaryotic lineages lack extremely well-conserved pathways, such as the absence of the anaphase promoting complex from Giardia (Gourguechon et al., 2013) or conserved kinetochore proteins from kinetoplasids (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Kinetoplasids lack conserved kinetochore proteins.
source: Our results may help to explain the surprising observation that certain eukaryotic lineages lack extremely well-conserved pathways, such as the absence of the anaphase promoting complex from Giardia (Gourguechon et al., 2013) or conserved kinetochore proteins from kinetoplasids (Akiyoshi and Gull, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In filamentous fungi, Cdc42 is not essential because its function is shared with Rac1.
source: In filamentous fungi, Cdc42 is not essential because its function is shared with Rac1 (Kwon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The deployment of the Cdc42 module and the Rac1 module for critical morphogenetic functions is surprisingly different between closely related fungal species.
source: However, the deployment of the Cdc42 module and the Rac1 module for critical morphogenetic functions is surprisingly different between closely related species (Harris, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Removing one component of a conserved pathway selects for the inactivation of others.
source: Our study shows that removing one component of a conserved pathway selects for the inactivation of others.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: If the process of inactivating pathway components was accompanied by the recruitment of novel proteins, it could ultimately lead to an evolutionary shift that replaced one module with another unrelated one that performed the same function.
source: If this process was accompanied by the recruitment of novel proteins, it could ultimately lead to an evolutionary shift that replaced one module with another unrelated one that performed the same function.
evidence: This is a speculation about long-term evolutionary consequences.

claim: Severely defective mutations could be fixed in population bottlenecks that accompany speciation.
source: There are ways of countering the objection: severely defective mutations could be fixed in population bottlenecks that accompany speciation
evidence: This is a speculation about how deleterious mutations could be fixed.

claim: Mutations that removed important components could be pleiotropic, offering advantages in novel environments similar in magnitude to the costs they impose on conserved core functions.
source: secondly, and maybe more likely, mutations that removed important components could be pleiotropic, offering advantages in novel environments that were similar in magnitude to the costs they impose on strongly conserved core functions
evidence: This is a speculation about how deleterious mutations could be fixed.

claim: Previously selected mutations in the same or related pathways could make the defects associated with the removal of a component less severe.
source: and thirdly, previously selected mutations in the same or related pathways could make the defects associated with the removal of a component less severe.
evidence: This is a speculation about how deleterious mutations could be fixed.

claim: There is evidence for the loss of widely conserved genes in individual evolutionary lineages.
source: These include the loss of widely conserved genes in individual evolutionary lineages (Bergmiller et al., 2012; Gourguechon et al., 2013; Drinnenberg et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 88 genes were lost in the descent of Saccharomyces cerevisiae from an ancestor that existed 100 Mya ago.
source: the loss of genes present in ancestral species during evolutionary diversification (e.g., the loss of 88 genes in the descent of Saccharomyces cerevisiae from an ancestor that existed 100 Mya ago [Gordon et al., 2009])
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Deciphering the physical mechanisms of polarity establishment in all the different combinations of mutants will teach us about evolution of functional modules.
source: Deciphering the physical mechanisms of polarity establishment in all the different combinations of mutants will teach us about evolution of functional modules.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Deciphering the physical mechanisms of polarity establishment in mutants will reveal more about cell biology of polarization.
source: However, it will also reveal more about cell biology of polarization.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: High-throughput studies have not shown physical or genetic interactions between NRP1 and any of the currently known polarity genes.
source: High-throughput studies, at least as indicated on the yeast genome website SGD (www.yeastgenome.org) have not shown physical or genetic interactions between NRP1 and any of the currently known polarity genes.
evidence: This is based on information from a database.

claim: The lack of information about NRP1 made it impossible to predict the positive effect of the BEM2 deletion on polarity establishment in the absence of BEM1 and BEM3.
source: However, the lack of information about NRP1 made it impossible to predict the positive effect of the BEM2 deletion on polarity establishment in the absence of BEM1 and BEM3.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of prior knowledge.

claim: It may be more important to alter quantitative parameters of the overall polarization process than to alter the behavior of a particular protein.
source: Cell polarization is a complicated, dynamical process, thus it may be more important to alter quantitative parameters of the overall process, regardless of the gene whose mutation produces the change, than it is to alter the behavior of a particular protein.
evidence: This is a speculation about the principles of polarization.

claim: The W303 strain background was used for all experiments.
source: The W303 strain background was used for all experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Standard rich media YPD was used for the evolution experiments.
source: Standard rich media, YPD (2% Peptone, 2% D–Glucose, and 1% Yeast-Extract) was used for the evolution experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Riboflavin and folic acid were not added to the YNB to minimize auto fluorescence.
source: The YNB was based on the recipe of Wickerham (1952), with the following modifications: riboflavin and folic acid were not added to the YNB to minimize auto fluorescence (Sheff and Thorn, 2004).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice supported by a citation.

claim: Approximately 20% of the colonies that grew on the selection plates were bem1∆.
source: Typically, ∼20% of the colonies were indeed bem1∆.
evidence: This is based on PCR verification of colonies.

claim: The other cells that grew on selection plates were most likely haploid MATa cells aneuploid for chromosome II containing both BEM1 and the selection marker.
source: The other cells were most likely haploid, MATa, cells, aneuploid for chromosome II and thus contained both BEM1 and the selection marker.
evidence: This is an inference about the genotype of non-bem1∆ colonies.

claim: One bem1∆ culture and three wild-type cultures were lost due to bacterial contamination early in the evolution experiment.
source: Early in the evolution experiment 1 bem1∆ culture and three wild-type cultures were lost due to bacterial contamination.
evidence: This describes what happened during the experiment.

claim: Line A2 got contaminated after 33 passages but was restarted from the frozen stock at passage 30 and was evolved for 820 generations.
source: The other cultures were all evolved for 1000 generations (100 passages), except for line A2 which got contaminated after 33 passages, but was restarted from the frozen stock at passage 30 and was evolved for 820 generation (82 passages).
evidence: This describes what happened during the experiment.

claim: Spa2-Citrine localizes to the polarity site and the cytokinetic ring.
source: Because there are large cytoplasmic pools of Cdc42, which make it hard to monitor the location of membrane-associated, active Cdc42, we examined polarization by imaging Spa2-Citrine, which localizes to the polarity site and the cytokinetic ring (Figure 4A,B, Video 4) (Snyder, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 4A,B and Video 4.

claim: All the bem1∆ colonies that survived in the spore plotting assay contained Spa2-Citrine, even though this allele was heterozygous in the diploid they were derived from.
source: The percentage of surviving bem1∆ colonies was higher in this assay than in the original assay (Figure 1A,B), which we attribute to the presence of Spa2-Citrine: all the bem1∆ colonies that survived contained Spa2-Citrine, even though this allele was heterozygous in the diploid that they were derived from.
evidence: This is an observation from the spore plotting assay.
